A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sequential monitoring framework, despite the changed title and layout. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–H support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix H report original simulations of normal-form games, Grid Soccer, and Predator-Prey, including detection times, empirical error rates, and sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation results and adds a population Rock-Paper-Scissors experiment comparing four detection procedures.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 replaces historical threshold crossings with comparisons against current e-process values. Section 2 explicitly stops all processes together at the first nonempty rejection set, replacing the earlier procedure with permanently accumulating rejections. This changes a central inference procedure, while the underlying payoff and likelihood-ratio constructions remain.

E1.justification: Appendix H.2 adds population Rock-Paper-Scissors, extending normal-form evaluation beyond the original two-player game to interactions where a biased minority changes the incentives of a compliant majority. This introduces a distinct population and payoff environment; the original normal-form and two gridworld scenarios remain.

E2.justification: The new population comparison evaluates Split-FWER and Split-FDR alongside the unscreened FWER and FDR procedures. These screening-based comparators were absent from v1; the existing experiments retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Appendix H.2 introduces a 3000-round protocol and a separate 50-round screening phase selecting 10 of 60 hypotheses before testing on subsequent observations. Section 4.1 also changes the stated significance level from 0.05 to 0.2, matching Appendix H.1 in both versions; this correction does not establish that the existing experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The population experiment adds controlled comparisons of screening versus no screening and a diagnostic analysis of which player-action hypotheses trigger detection. The existing betting-parameter sensitivity analysis, null-error checks, unknown-deviation robustness experiment, and gridworld case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v3 specifies 200 independent trials for the new population experiment. Existing repetition counts, including 300 normal-form runs and 150 Grid Soccer trials per deviation magnitude, and Figure 7's interquartile reporting remain unchanged. This is additional repetition information, not an increase in runs for existing experiments.

E6.justification: New Figure 8 reports population-game mean detection times of 2025, 1248, 1438, and 802 rounds for FWER, FDR, Split-FWER, and Split-FDR, respectively, alongside detection distributions and hypothesis-level findings. Figure 1 also changes the FDR mean from 1545 to 1546 while retaining FWER at 1765; the FDR procedure itself changed, so this is not a same-method performance comparison.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.8 and Appendix C.5 replace the guarantee for historical-crossing rejection sets at arbitrary stopping times with a guarantee at the common first-alarm stopping time. The proof replaces conditioning Ville's inequality on the data-dependent rejection count with optional stopping, Fatou's lemma, and an e-BH inequality. Appendix D also revises the conditioning filtration and explicitly counts action-pair hypotheses.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion now distinguish equilibrium testing in normal-form games from compliance testing against a specified policy in stochastic games. The introduction removes the claim of requiring no stationary distributions. These qualify the headline scope to better match the existing technical formulation; the principal monitoring and detection-power contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 explains why population-game detections concentrate on compliant players with profitable deviations rather than identify the agents causing the imbalance. It also discusses screening's discarded-observation and missed-signal costs, and removes the earlier interpretation emphasizing permanently remembered threshold crossings. The main limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix H.2 documents the population payoff matrix, uniform and Rock-biased strategies, and screening implementation. Section 4.1 changes the code-repository address from betting-equilibrium to anytime-detection-deviation. Existing gridworld solver, smoothing, and environment details are retained.

R1.justification: v3 removes Tavyrikov et al. (2025) and positions the revised FDR procedure as standard e-BH from Wang and Ramdas (2022) applied to jointly stopped e-values. Appendix A adds Velasco et al. (2025), explicitly acknowledging parallels with token-auditing estimators and detection bounds. Most related-work positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes, and selected passages in the abstract, FDR explanation, stochastic-game introduction, and discussion are rewritten. Notation explanations and an Impact Statement are added. The main section sequence and most appendix exposition remain intact, with a new H.2 subsection inserted before the stochastic experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with extensively resized and repositioned displays and new running headers. Figure 8 adds a four-panel population comparison, Figure 5 updates stopping-time markers, and several axes adopt 'Supermartingale' terminology. Existing gameplay figures and tables are retained despite relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 repairs an important deficiency in the central FDR contribution: Algorithm 2 and Appendix C.5 replace historical-crossing decisions and an unjustified conditional application of Ville's inequality with current e-values at a common stopping time and a matching proof. Although the stated guarantee is narrower, it is better supported. The population experiment, screening comparisons, and clearer distinction between equilibrium testing and policy compliance further strengthen the evidence and precision.
